strand.title: Number
strand.metaDescription: GCSE number: structure and calculation, fractions, decimals and percentages, measures and accuracy.

topics.title: Structure and calculation

subtopics.title: Place value in integers and decimals
subtopics.description: What each digit is worth in integers and decimals, and zeros as place-holders.
subtopics.coverNote: Digit values in integers to millions and decimals to thousandths; zeros as place-holders; writing numbers in words and figures; stating the value of a named digit. Ordering and comparing live on the sibling ordering-numbers page; rounding lives on Measures and accuracy. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Ordering integers, decimals and negatives
subtopics.description: Ordering numbers, including negatives and decimals of different lengths.
subtopics.coverNote: Ordering integers, decimals of different lengths and negatives, ascending and descending, with number-line placement; padding decimals to equal length; temperature contexts. The symbols themselves live on inequality-symbols; ordering fractions and percentages lives in the FDP topic; standard-form ordering has its own page. Both tiers. (N1)

subtopics.title: The inequality symbols
subtopics.description: The less-than, greater-than, at-most, at-least and not-equal signs.
subtopics.coverNote: Reading and writing the six DfE symbols =, not-equal, <, >, at-most and at-least between numbers, including negatives and decimals; which two allow equality; listing integers satisfying a statement like -2 < n at-most 3. Solving inequalities is Algebra; error-interval notation lives on Measures. Both tiers. (N1)

subtopics.title: Multiplying and dividing by powers of ten
subtopics.description: The effect on every digit of multiplying or dividing by 10, 100, 0.1 and 0.01.
subtopics.coverNote: Multiplying and dividing integers and decimals by 10, 100, 1000, 0.1 and 0.01 as shifts of every digit, including why dividing by 0.1 enlarges. Exclude index notation for powers of ten (standard-form page) and metric conversion (Measures). Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Column addition
subtopics.description: Adding integers and decimals in columns, lining up the point and carrying.
subtopics.coverNote: Column addition of integers and decimals of different lengths, carrying between columns, aligning the point, padding with zeros; money and measure contexts. Subtraction lives on column-subtraction; estimation checks live on Measures; negative operands live on adding-subtracting-negatives. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Column subtraction
subtopics.description: Subtracting in columns with exchange, lining up decimals of different lengths.
subtopics.coverNote: Column subtraction of integers and decimals with exchange, aligning points and padding shorter decimals, e.g. 12 - 3.475; change and difference contexts. Exchanges that must pass through zero digits get the sibling page; answers below zero live on adding-subtracting-negatives. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Exchanging across zeros
subtopics.description: Subtracting when a column holds a zero, and where the exchange comes from.
subtopics.coverNote: Subtractions like 4.03 - 1.276 and 3000 - 847 where the exchange must travel through one or more zeros, showing where each borrowed unit comes from and the reindexed digits. Assumes column-subtraction; do not reteach basic single-column exchange here. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Long multiplication
subtopics.description: Multiplying multi-digit integers, and the place-holder zero in the second row.
subtopics.coverNote: Long multiplication of two- and three-digit integers with the place-holder zero in each later row; grid method as backup; worded cost and area contexts. Decimal operands live on multiplying-decimals; estimation as a check lives on Measures estimating-calculations. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Multiplying decimals
subtopics.description: Multiplying as whole numbers, then counting decimal places to fix the point.
subtopics.coverNote: Multiplying decimals via the integer product then counting decimal places, e.g. 0.3 x 0.4 = 0.12, with a unit-square area model for that case; setting the columns out as whole numbers rather than aligning the points; tidying a trailing zero only after the count is made. Assumes long-multiplication; estimation as a check lives on Measures estimating-calculations; division by decimals lives on dividing-by-decimals; the general rule for when a product shrinks lives on numbers-below-one in the FDP topic. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Short division
subtopics.description: Dividing by a one-digit number, carrying each remainder into the next digit.
subtopics.coverNote: Short division of integers and decimals by one-digit divisors, carrying remainders into the next digit and continuing past the point for exact decimal answers. Deciding what a leftover means lives on interpreting-remainders; two-digit divisors live on long-division. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Interpreting a remainder
subtopics.description: Whether a worded answer wants a remainder, a decimal, a fraction or rounding.
subtopics.coverNote: Worded division answers: choosing between remainder form, exact decimal, fraction, and rounding up or down in context (coaches, boxes, tickets). One-digit divisors here; the context-forced rounding direction recurs on Measures rounding-in-context, so cross-reference rather than duplicate. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Long division
subtopics.description: Dividing by a two-digit number, continuing past the point for an exact answer.
subtopics.coverNote: Long division by two-digit divisors, integer and decimal dividends, continuing past the point for exact decimal answers; layout, subtracting multiples, and a listed multiples crib. Decimal divisors live on dividing-by-decimals; remainder interpretation lives on interpreting-remainders. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Dividing by a decimal
subtopics.description: Scaling both numbers by the same power of ten, and why the answer can grow.
subtopics.coverNote: Rewriting divisions like 55.2 / 0.46 by scaling both numbers by the same power of ten until the divisor is an integer, and why the quotient can exceed the dividend. Assumes short and long division; the size intuition cross-references numbers-below-one in FDP. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Using a given calculation
subtopics.description: Related products and quotients from a stated result, without recalculating.
subtopics.coverNote: From a stated fact like 43 x 26 = 1118, deducing related products, quotients and missing factors such as 4.3 x 2.6 and 1118 / 4.3 by tracking powers of ten; no recalculating. Estimating unrelated calculations lives on Measures estimating-calculations. Both tiers. (N2, N3)

subtopics.title: Index notation and powers
subtopics.description: What the base and index mean, and writing repeated multiplication as a power.
subtopics.coverNote: Meaning of base and index for positive integer powers; writing repeated multiplication as a power and back; evaluating squares, cubes and small powers like 2 to the 5 without a calculator. The index laws live in their own group; algebraic indices live in Algebra. Both tiers. (N6)

subtopics.title: Recognising powers of a number
subtopics.description: The squares, cubes and powers of 2, 3, 4 and 5 worth recalling.
subtopics.coverNote: Recognising powers of 2, 3, 4 and 5, which N6 names explicitly; squares to 15 squared and cubes of 1 to 5 and 10; writing 64 as a power of 2, 4 or 8. Estimating roots of non-powers lives on Measures estimating-roots. Both tiers. (N6)

subtopics.title: Square roots
subtopics.description: The square root as the inverse of squaring, found by reversing a known square.
subtopics.coverNote: The square root as the inverse of squaring; roots of perfect squares to 225 and of decimals like root 0.25, non-calculator. The two-solution issue lives on positive-and-negative-roots; estimating irrational roots lives on Measures estimating-roots; surd manipulation is Higher, in the surds group. Both tiers. (N6, N7)

subtopics.title: Positive and negative square roots
subtopics.description: Why a squared equation has two solutions while the root sign gives one.
subtopics.coverNote: Why x squared = k has two solutions while the root sign denotes only the positive one; plus-or-minus notation; giving both roots of 49. Solving quadratic equations lives in Algebra; roots of negatives have no real value at GCSE, and complex numbers are A level. Both tiers. (N6)

subtopics.title: Cube roots and higher roots
subtopics.description: Cube roots and nth roots as the inverse of a power, including negatives.
subtopics.coverNote: Cube roots of perfect cubes including negatives like the cube root of -27, and higher roots such as the fifth root of 32, as inverses of powers; calculator root keys. Fractional-index notation for roots is Higher, on unit-fractional-indices; estimation lives on Measures. Both tiers. (N6, N7)

subtopics.title: Adding and subtracting negative numbers
subtopics.description: Number-line reasoning, two signs meeting, and temperature differences.
subtopics.coverNote: Adding and subtracting directed numbers, integers and decimals, including double signs like 5 - (-3); number-line reasoning; temperature and bank-balance differences. Products and quotients live on multiplying-dividing-negatives; negative fractions live in the FDP topic. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Multiplying and dividing negative numbers
subtopics.description: The sign of a product or quotient, and what several negatives together do.
subtopics.coverNote: Sign rules for products and quotients of negatives, integers and decimals, including chains of three or more factors and mixed sign counts. Powers of negatives get their own page; negative indices are a different idea entirely, on negative-indices. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Order of operations
subtopics.description: Brackets, powers and roots first, with the fraction bar as grouping.
subtopics.coverNote: Evaluating multi-step calculations with brackets, indices, roots and the four operations; the fraction bar and root sign as implicit grouping; N3 names reciprocals within priority notation, so include them. Calculator keying lives on calculator-methods; algebraic substitution lives in Algebra. Both tiers. (N3)

subtopics.title: Powers of a negative number
subtopics.description: Why −3² and (−3)² differ, and how an odd or even index fixes the sign.
subtopics.coverNote: Why -3 squared and (-3) squared differ, and how an odd or even index fixes the sign; evaluating powers like (-2) to the 4 without a calculator. Assumes index-notation and the sign rules; substitution errors with x squared live in Algebra. Both tiers. (N2, N3, N6)

subtopics.title: Checking an answer with the inverse operation
subtopics.description: Undoing a calculation with its inverse to test an answer without repeating it.
subtopics.coverNote: Checking a completed calculation by the inverse operation, across the four operations and powers against roots; choosing which inverse statement verifies a given result. Estimation-based checking lives on Measures checking-answers; regrouping for easier arithmetic lives on reordering-a-calculation. Both tiers. (N3)

subtopics.title: Reordering a calculation
subtopics.description: Using commutativity and associativity to pair the easiest numbers first.
subtopics.coverNote: Using commutativity and associativity to regroup sums and products, like 4 x 17 x 25, and cancellation to simplify before calculating; recognising that subtraction and division cannot be reordered freely. Law names optional; algebraic manipulation lives in Algebra. Both tiers. (N3)

subtopics.title: Factors and factor pairs
subtopics.description: Listing every factor of a number in pairs, so none is missed or repeated.
subtopics.coverNote: Listing every factor of numbers to about 100 in ordered pairs so none is missed; factor and divisor vocabulary; square numbers having an odd factor count. Divisibility tests live on multiples-and-divisibility; counting factors from indices lives on counting-factors. Both tiers. (N4)

subtopics.title: Multiples and divisibility tests
subtopics.description: The multiples of a number, and the tests for divisibility by 2, 3, 4, 5 and 9.
subtopics.coverNote: Multiples and common multiples, and the divisibility tests for 2, 3, 4, 5, 9 and 10 applied to three- and four-digit numbers. LCM method lives on lcm-from-prime-factors; primality testing by trial division lives on primes-and-primality. Both tiers. (N4)

subtopics.title: Primes and testing for primality
subtopics.description: What makes a number prime, why 1 is not, and trial division up to the root.
subtopics.coverNote: The definition of prime, why 1 is excluded, identifying primes to 50, and testing numbers like 91, 97 and 117 by trial division by primes up to the square root. Prime factorisation lives on the next page; infinitude-of-primes proofs are A level. Both tiers. (N4)

subtopics.title: Prime factorisation
subtopics.description: Factor trees and repeated division, index form, and why the primes are unique.
subtopics.coverNote: Writing numbers up to four digits as products of primes by factor tree or repeated division, answered in index form; N4 names product notation and the unique factorisation theorem, so state uniqueness. HCF, LCM and square-making applications live on their own pages. Both tiers. (N4)

subtopics.title: Highest common factor
subtopics.description: Taking each shared prime to the lower index, and what the HCF means.
subtopics.coverNote: HCF of two numbers beyond 100 from index-form prime factorisations, taking each shared prime to its lower index; what HCF means; listing method as backup for small numbers. LCM is the sibling page; three numbers and Venn diagrams live on hcf-lcm-venn. Both tiers. (N4)

subtopics.title: Lowest common multiple
subtopics.description: Every prime to the higher index, and why the LCM is not always the product.
subtopics.coverNote: LCM from prime factorisations, taking every prime to its higher index; why the LCM is at most the product and equals it only for coprime numbers; listing multiples as backup. Worded HCF-or-LCM decisions live on choosing-hcf-or-lcm. Both tiers. (N4)

subtopics.title: HCF and LCM from a Venn diagram
subtopics.description: The Venn method for two or three numbers, and HCF times LCM as the product.
subtopics.coverNote: The Venn-diagram method for HCF and LCM of two or three numbers, and HCF x LCM = product for two numbers, including finding a missing number from the other three values. Assumes both prime-factor pages; formal set notation lives in Probability, not here. Both tiers. (N4)

subtopics.title: Choosing HCF or LCM in context
subtopics.description: Deciding which a worded problem needs: coinciding events or equal shares.
subtopics.coverNote: Worded problems deciding between HCF and LCM: buses coinciding, largest equal tiles or shares, gear teeth, packs matching; extracting the numbers and naming the decision. Calculation methods assumed from the earlier pages; pure computation questions stay there. Both tiers. (N4)

subtopics.title: Squares and cubes from prime factors
subtopics.description: The smallest multiplier that turns a number into a perfect square or cube.
subtopics.coverNote: Finding the smallest multiplier, or divisor, that turns a number into a perfect square or cube by making every index even or a multiple of three. Assumes index-form factorisation; counting factors lives on counting-factors; recognising squares and cubes lives on recognising-powers. Both tiers. (N4, N6)

subtopics.title: Counting a number’s factors
subtopics.description: Counting a number’s factors from the indices in its prime factorisation.
subtopics.coverNote: Counting a number's factors by adding one to each index in the prime factorisation and multiplying; why square numbers have an odd count. An extension beyond N4's wording, so keep questions short and Higher-leaning; direct listing lives on factors-and-factor-pairs. Both tiers. (N4)

subtopics.title: Systematic listing
subtopics.description: Listing every outcome once in a fixed order, and deciding whether order matters.
subtopics.coverNote: Listing outcomes once each in a fixed order: two-digit numbers from given digits, menu pairs, team match-ups; deciding whether order matters; counting from the finished list. The multiplicative shortcut is Higher-only on product-rule-counting; probabilities from sample spaces live in Probability. Both tiers. (N5)

subtopics.title: The product rule for counting
subtopics.description: Multiplying the choices at each stage, including arrangements without reuse.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, N5's braced clause. Multiplying choice counts across independent stages: codes, menus, outfits; arrangements without repetition where choices shrink slot by slot; restrictions like a fixed first digit. Factorial and nCr notation are A level; Foundation counts by exhaustive listing on systematic-listing. (N5)

subtopics.title: Multiplying powers of the same base
subtopics.description: Adding the indices, derived by counting the repeated factors on each side.
subtopics.coverNote: Adding indices when multiplying powers of the same numeric base, derived by counting repeated factors, e.g. 3 to the 4 times 3 squared; three-factor chains included. Different bases never combine; division is the sibling page; algebraic bases live on the Algebra notation page. Both tiers. (N7)

subtopics.title: Dividing powers of the same base
subtopics.description: Subtracting the indices, derived by cancelling the common repeated factors.
subtopics.coverNote: Subtracting indices when dividing powers of the same numeric base, derived by cancelling repeated factors; keep results at positive indices here, handing subtractions that give zero or negative answers to zero-index and negative-indices. Algebraic bases live in Algebra. Both tiers. (N7)

subtopics.title: The zero index
subtopics.description: Why any non-zero number to the power zero is 1, read off the division law.
subtopics.coverNote: Why any non-zero base to the power zero is 1, read off the division law and the dividing-down pattern; evaluating mixtures like 7 to the 0 times 5 cubed. Zero to the zero stays out of scope; negative indices follow on the sibling page. Both tiers. (N7)

subtopics.title: Negative indices
subtopics.description: A negative index as a reciprocal, making a number small rather than negative.
subtopics.coverNote: A negative integer index as the reciprocal of the positive power, e.g. 2 to the -3 is 1/8; why results are small, not negative; numeric bases only. Foundation and Higher both examine integer indices; fractional indices are Higher, on the later trio of pages. (N7)

subtopics.title: A negative index on a fraction
subtopics.description: Inverting the fraction first, then applying the positive index.
subtopics.coverNote: Evaluating a fraction to a negative index by inverting first then applying the positive index, e.g. (2/3) to the -2 is 9/4; mixed numbers converted first. Assumes negative-indices and the quotient rule from power-of-a-product; fractional indices on fractions are Higher, on negative-fractional-indices. Both tiers. (N7)

subtopics.title: Raising a power to a power
subtopics.description: Multiplying the indices, and telling this apart from multiplying powers.
subtopics.coverNote: Multiplying indices when raising a power to a power, e.g. (2 cubed) to the 4, explicitly contrasted with 2 cubed times 2 to the 4; combined-law simplifications with numeric bases. Justifies fractional indices later at Higher; algebraic versions live on the Algebra notation page. Both tiers. (N7)

subtopics.title: Powers of a product and a quotient
subtopics.description: Applying an index to every factor in a bracket and both parts of a fraction.
subtopics.coverNote: Applying one index across a product and across a quotient: (2 x 5) cubed and (3/4) squared, numeric bases only; combining with earlier laws in one simplification. Teach before negative-index-of-a-fraction, which uses the quotient case. Algebraic brackets like (2x cubed) squared live in Algebra. Both tiers. (N7)

subtopics.title: Index equations and changing the base
subtopics.description: Writing both sides as powers of one base, then equating the indices.
subtopics.coverNote: Solving equations like 2 to the x = 32 and 2 to the x times 4 = 2 to the 7 by writing both sides over one base and equating indices; bases 2, 3, 5 and 10. Beyond N7's explicit wording, so keep it brief; logarithms are A level. Both tiers. (N6, N7)

subtopics.title: Unit fractional indices
subtopics.description: The index one over n as the nth root, derived from raising a power to a power.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, N7's braced clause. The index 1/n as the nth root, justified by raising a power to a power; evaluating 25 to the 1/2, 27 to the 1/3, 32 to the 1/5 without a calculator. General m/n indices follow next; Foundation stops at integer indices. (N7)

subtopics.title: Fractional indices
subtopics.description: The index m over n as a root and a power, and which one to take first.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Evaluating a to the m/n as nth root first then mth power, e.g. 27 to the 2/3 is 9, with bases that are perfect powers; converting between root and index notation both ways. Negative fractional indices follow on the sibling page; Foundation stops at integer indices. (N7)

subtopics.title: Negative fractional indices
subtopics.description: Combining reciprocal, root and power in the order that keeps numbers small.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Combining reciprocal, root and power to evaluate 8 to the -2/3 or (25/16) to the -1/2, rooting first to keep numbers small and inverting fractional bases first. Assumes every earlier index page; equations with unknown fractional indices belong to A level. (N7)

subtopics.title: Standard form
subtopics.description: Converting both ways for large and small numbers, and correcting near-misses.
subtopics.coverNote: Converting both ways between ordinary numbers and A x 10 to the n with 1 at-most A < 10 and integer n, large and small; correcting near-misses like 34 x 10 to the 5; real contexts. Ordering and arithmetic live on the three sibling pages; calculator entry lives on calculator-standard-form. Both tiers. (N9)

subtopics.title: Ordering numbers in standard form
subtopics.description: Comparing by the power of ten first, then by the front number.
subtopics.coverNote: Ordering and comparing values in standard form by power of ten first, then front number, with mixed lists containing ordinary numbers converted first; negative powers ordering counterintuitively. Conversion assumed from standard-form; calculation lives on the multiply-divide and add-subtract siblings. Both tiers. (N1, N9)

subtopics.title: Multiplying and dividing in standard form
subtopics.description: Products, quotients and how-many-times-bigger comparisons.
subtopics.coverNote: Multiplying and dividing in standard form without a calculator via the index laws, renormalising fronts like 40 x 10 to the 7; how-many-times-larger comparisons in astronomy and cell contexts. Addition lives on the sibling page; calculator methods live on calculator-standard-form. Both tiers. (N9)

subtopics.title: Adding and subtracting in standard form
subtopics.description: Matching the powers of ten before combining, then renormalising the result.
subtopics.coverNote: Adding and subtracting in standard form by matching the powers of ten, or converting to ordinary numbers, then renormalising the result; combined-population contexts. Products and quotients live on the sibling page; rounding answers to significant figures lives on Measures. Both tiers. (N9)

subtopics.title: Entering a calculation on a calculator
subtopics.description: Brackets, fractions, powers, roots and negatives keyed as written.
subtopics.coverNote: Keying multi-step expressions on a scientific calculator: bracketing fraction-bar numerators and denominators, powers, roots, negatives, the fraction key; reading the display back. Standard-form entry and exact-value toggling get sibling pages; how much to round lives on Measures choosing-accuracy. Both tiers. (N3, N14)

subtopics.title: Standard form on a calculator
subtopics.description: The times-ten-to-the-power key, and reading answers off the display.
subtopics.coverNote: Entering standard-form values with the times-ten-to-the-power key, reading display output like 2.5E-3 back into standard form, and never writing calculator notation as an answer. Assumes standard-form conversion; non-calculator standard-form arithmetic lives on the standard-form sibling pages. Both tiers. (N9, N14)

subtopics.title: Exact values, ANS and memory
subtopics.description: Toggling between an exact value and its decimal, and reading the full display.
subtopics.coverNote: Toggling between exact display (fraction, root, pi) and decimal with the S-to-D key, and reading the whole display before rounding. Only the toggle lives here: when exactness is demanded lives on exact-answers, and the ANS and memory keys live on calculator-ans-memory. Both tiers. (N8, N14)

subtopics.title: The answer and memory keys
subtopics.description: Carrying a full unrounded value into the next step, not a retyped rounded one.
subtopics.coverNote: Using the ANS and memory keys to carry full unrounded values through chained calculations rather than retyping rounded ones; two-step problems where early rounding visibly corrupts the result. Why premature rounding fails lives on Measures premature-rounding; cross-reference rather than duplicate. Both tiers. (N14)

subtopics.title: Exact answers and multiples of π
subtopics.description: Holding π, a fraction or a root as a symbol rather than a decimal.
subtopics.coverNote: Leaving answers as fractions or multiples of pi rather than rounded decimals, which N8 requires at both tiers; recognising exact values beside rounded lookalikes like 1/3 versus 0.333. Exact surd answers are Higher, in the surds group; the calculator toggle lives on calculator-exact-values. (N8)

subtopics.title: Rational and irrational numbers
subtopics.description: Which numbers are one integer over another, and where π and surds sit.
subtopics.coverNote: Definitions and classification: rational as one integer over another, including integers, terminating and recurring decimals; pi and non-square roots as irrational; deciding for root(9/16) and root 0.25. Foundation needs the vocabulary and examples; Higher links to surds. Irrationality proofs are A level. (N8, N10)

subtopics.title: Simplifying surds
subtopics.description: Extracting the largest square factor to write a√b, and comparing surds.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, N8's braced clause. Extracting the largest square factor to write root 12 as 2 root 3, reversing to compare surd sizes, and N8's own example root 12 = root 4 times root 3. Surd arithmetic lives on the sibling pages; Foundation never meets surds. (N8)

subtopics.title: Adding and subtracting surds
subtopics.description: Collecting like surds after simplifying every term.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Collecting like surds after simplifying every term, e.g. root 12 + root 27 = 5 root 3; unlike surds cannot combine, and root a + root b is not root(a+b). Assumes simplifying-surds; bracketed expressions live on expanding-surds. (N8)

subtopics.title: Multiplying surds
subtopics.description: Multiplying roots and coefficients separately, then simplifying the result.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Using root a times root b = root(ab), multiplying integer coefficients and roots separately, then simplifying the resulting surd, e.g. 2 root 3 times 5 root 6 = 30 root 2. Squaring and division get sibling pages; brackets live on expanding-surds. (N8)

subtopics.title: Squaring a surd
subtopics.description: Why a root times itself gives the number back, and what a coefficient does.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Why root a times root a returns a, and (k root a) squared = k squared a; instant evaluation without expanding digits. This is the rule rationalising and expanding depend on, so drill it alone; two-term squares like (1 + root 2) squared live on expanding-surds. (N8)

subtopics.title: Dividing surds
subtopics.description: Dividing under a single root, and simplifying quotients with coefficients.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Using root a over root b = root(a/b), simplifying quotients with integer coefficients like 6 root 20 over 2 root 5, and choosing whether to combine under one root first. Fractions whose surd denominator will not cancel move to rationalising-denominators. (N8)

subtopics.title: Expanding brackets with surds
subtopics.description: Single and double brackets, squaring one, and the difference of two squares.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Expanding single and double brackets containing surds, squaring binomials like (3 + root 2) squared, and the difference of two squares giving rational answers; exact perimeter and area contexts. Assumes the multiplying and squaring pages; conjugate rationalising builds on this next. (N8)

subtopics.title: Rationalising a denominator
subtopics.description: Clearing a single surd from the bottom of a fraction by multiplying by one.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only; N8 names rationalising denominators. Clearing a single-surd denominator by multiplying top and bottom by the surd, e.g. 5 over root 3 becomes 5 root 3 over 3, simplifying afterwards. Two-term denominators live on rationalising-conjugates; answers stay exact, never decimal. (N8)

subtopics.title: Rationalising with a conjugate
subtopics.description: Clearing a two-term surd denominator by reversing the middle sign and expanding.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher extension. Clearing a two-term denominator like 1 over (3 - root 2) by multiplying by the conjugate, the difference of two squares making the bottom rational. N8 names rationalising but not conjugates, so pitch as grade 8-9 stretch and A level preparation. Assumes expanding-surds. (N8)

topics.metaDescription: GCSE fractions, decimals and percentages: equivalence and ordering, the four operations, converting between the three forms, and percentage change.
topics.practiceLead: The drill below runs the four operations across proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers.

subtopics.title: A fraction as a division
subtopics.description: The fraction bar read as a division, and any integer written as a fraction.
subtopics.coverNote: The fraction bar read as division: a/b equals a divided by b, converting 3/4 into a division and back; any integer written over 1; sharing contexts like three pizzas among four. Number-line placement and decimal conversion live on later pages; no arithmetic on fractions yet. Both tiers. (N2, N10)

subtopics.title: Fractions on a number line
subtopics.description: Placing a fraction or mixed number by splitting each unit into equal parts.
subtopics.coverNote: Placing proper fractions and mixed numbers on a number line by splitting each unit interval into equal parts, and reading marked points back off; halves through tenths; a brief look at negatives. Full ordering methods live on ordering-fractions and ordering-negatives. Both tiers. (N1)

subtopics.title: Equivalent fractions and simplest form
subtopics.description: Scaling numerator and denominator together, and cancelling to simplest form.
subtopics.coverNote: Generating equivalent fractions by scaling numerator and denominator together, cancelling to simplest form with the HCF, denominators to about 100; recognising equivalence in diagrams. Comparing and ordering live on ordering-fractions; equivalent ratios and fractions in ratio problems live in the Ratio strand. Both tiers. (N1, N2)

subtopics.title: Improper fractions and mixed numbers
subtopics.description: Converting between improper fractions and mixed numbers, and when to use each.
subtopics.coverNote: Converting both ways between improper fractions and mixed numbers, and when each form is useful: mixed for judging size, improper for calculating. Assumes fraction-as-division; arithmetic on mixed numbers lives in the calculating group; negative mixed numbers wait for the negative-fractions pages. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Comparing and ordering fractions
subtopics.description: Ordering fractions by common denominator, common numerator or benchmarking.
subtopics.coverNote: Comparing two fractions and ordering lists by common denominator, common numerator, or benchmarking against a half and one; denominators to 24. Stating results symbolically lives on comparison-symbols; mixed fraction-decimal-percentage lists live on ordering-fdp; negatives live on ordering-negatives. Both tiers. (N1)

subtopics.title: Comparison symbols
subtopics.description: Stating a comparison with the equality and inequality symbols.
subtopics.coverNote: Recording comparisons with all six N1 symbols: equals, not-equal, less-than, greater-than, at-most, at-least, applied to fractions, decimals and percentages; which two permit equality. Ordering whole lists lives on the ordering pages; solving algebraic inequalities lives in Algebra. Both tiers. (N1)

subtopics.title: Adding and subtracting fractions
subtopics.description: Adding and subtracting fractions with like and unlike denominators.
subtopics.coverNote: Adding and subtracting proper and improper fractions, like denominators then unlike via the LCM; simplifying answers; confronting the add-tops-and-bottoms error directly. Mixed numbers live on adding-mixed-numbers; negatives live on adding-subtracting-negative-fractions; word problems kept to same-unit quantities. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Adding and subtracting mixed numbers
subtopics.description: Adding and subtracting mixed numbers, including exchange from the whole part.
subtopics.coverNote: Adding and subtracting mixed numbers, wholes and parts separately or via improper fractions, including subtractions needing exchange from the whole, like 3 1/4 minus 1 2/3; measurement contexts. Assumes adding-fractions and mixed-numbers; products and quotients live on multiplying-dividing-mixed-numbers. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Multiplying fractions
subtopics.description: Multiplying fractions by fractions or integers, cancelling before multiplying.
subtopics.coverNote: Multiplying fraction by fraction and fraction by integer, cancelling common factors before multiplying; fraction-of-a-fraction and area contexts; why a product can be smaller than either factor. Mixed numbers live on the mixed-numbers arithmetic page; the shrinking idea deepens on numbers-below-one. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Reciprocals
subtopics.description: The reciprocal of an integer, fraction or mixed number.
subtopics.coverNote: The reciprocal of an integer, fraction, mixed number and decimal; a number times its reciprocal makes 1; zero has no reciprocal. N3 names reciprocals in priority-of-operations notation. Division by fractions applies this on dividing-fractions; negative indices as reciprocals live on the structure topic. Both tiers. (N2, N3)

subtopics.title: Dividing fractions
subtopics.description: Dividing by a fraction or an integer by multiplying by the reciprocal.
subtopics.coverNote: Dividing a fraction by a fraction or integer, and an integer by a fraction, by multiplying by the reciprocal, with a how-many-fit diagram justifying the rule. Assumes reciprocals; mixed numbers live on the next page; sign rules live on the negative-fraction pages. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Multiplying and dividing mixed numbers
subtopics.description: Multiplying and dividing mixed numbers by converting to improper fractions.
subtopics.coverNote: Multiplying and dividing mixed numbers by converting to improper fractions first, cancelling before multiplying, converting back at the end; recipe and area contexts. This page anchors the fraction-arithmetic drill. Addition with exchange lives on adding-mixed-numbers; negatives live on the sibling pages. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Adding and subtracting negative fractions
subtopics.description: Where the sign sits in a negative mixed number, and subtracting a negative.
subtopics.coverNote: Adding and subtracting negative fractions and mixed numbers: where the sign sits, combining directed-number rules with common denominators, and subtracting a negative. Assumes adding-fractions plus the structure topic's directed-number pages; products and quotients live on multiplying-dividing-negative-fractions. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Multiplying and dividing negative fractions
subtopics.description: The sign rules applied to products and quotients of negative fractions.
subtopics.coverNote: Applying the sign rules to products and quotients of negative fractions and mixed numbers, including chains with several negative factors and squaring a negative fraction. Assumes multiplying-fractions, dividing-fractions and multiplying-dividing-negatives; powers of positive fractions live on powers-of-fractions. Both tiers. (N2)

subtopics.title: Powers and roots of fractions
subtopics.description: Squaring, cubing and rooting a fraction, numerator and denominator separately.
subtopics.coverNote: Squaring, cubing and square-rooting fractions by treating numerator and denominator separately, e.g. (2/3) squared and root(9/16); why powering a proper fraction shrinks it. Negative and fractional indices live on the structure topic, fractional ones Higher; decimals live on powers-of-decimals. Both tiers. (N6, N7)

subtopics.title: Powers and roots of decimals
subtopics.description: Squaring, cubing and rooting decimals, and why 0.3 squared is not 0.9.
subtopics.coverNote: Squaring, cubing and rooting decimals via the integer power and decimal-place counting: 0.3 squared is 0.09 not 0.9, root 0.36 is 0.6; predicting size first. Assumes multiplying-decimals on the structure topic; estimating roots of arbitrary numbers lives on Measures estimating-roots. Both tiers. (N6)

subtopics.title: Multiplying and dividing by numbers below one
subtopics.description: How multiplying or dividing by a number below one changes a quantity.
subtopics.coverNote: The size effects of multiplying or dividing by a number between 0 and 1, fraction or decimal: multiplying shrinks, dividing enlarges; which-is-bigger judgements and estimation checks, no new algorithms. Underpins dividing-by-decimals and over-under-estimates; cross-reference both rather than reteach. Both tiers. (N2, N14)

subtopics.title: Finding a fraction of a quantity
subtopics.description: Dividing by the denominator and multiplying by the numerator.
subtopics.coverNote: Finding a fraction of a quantity by dividing by the denominator then multiplying by the numerator, non-calculator; money and measure contexts; comparisons like 2/5 of 40 against 1/3 of 36. Recovering the whole lives on finding-the-whole; percentage operators live in the percentages group. Both tiers. (N12)

subtopics.title: Finding the whole from a fraction
subtopics.description: Recovering the whole quantity when only a stated fraction of it is known.
subtopics.coverNote: Recovering a whole quantity when a stated fraction of it is known: if 3/5 of a number is 24, one part is 8; unitary reasoning and bar models. The percentage twin lives on reverse-percentage; fractions inside ratio problems live in the Ratio strand under N11. Both tiers. (N12)

subtopics.title: Writing one quantity as a fraction of another
subtopics.description: Writing one quantity as a fraction of another in the same units.
subtopics.coverNote: Writing one quantity as a fraction of another after converting to common units, e.g. 35 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours, simplifying fully; results above 1 allowed. The percentage version lives on quantity-as-percentage; ratio notation and sharing live in the Ratio strand. Both tiers. (N12)

subtopics.title: Converting a fraction to a decimal
subtopics.description: Converting a fraction to a decimal by short division.
subtopics.coverNote: Converting fractions to decimals by short division, e.g. 3/8 = 0.375, including N10's cited pairs like 7/2 = 3.5; fluency with halves, quarters, fifths, eighths and tenths. Recurring outputs take dot notation on recurring-decimal-notation; the reverse direction lives on decimals-to-fractions. Both tiers. (N10)

subtopics.title: Recurring decimal notation
subtopics.description: Dot notation for the repeating block, and writing it back out in digits.
subtopics.coverNote: Dot notation: one dot over a single repeating digit, dots over the first and last digits of a longer block; expanding dotted forms back into digit strings and recognising equal values. Predicting which fractions recur lives on the sibling pages; converting recurring decimals to fractions is Higher. Both tiers. (N10)

subtopics.title: Which fractions terminate
subtopics.description: Predicting from the denominator’s prime factors whether a fraction terminates.
subtopics.coverNote: Predicting from the simplified denominator's prime factors whether a fraction terminates or recurs: only 2s and 5s terminate; testing 3/8, 7/30 and 9/12 without dividing. Assumes prime factorisation from the structure topic; the underlying remainder argument lives on why-decimals-recur. Both tiers. (N10)

subtopics.title: Why every fraction terminates or recurs
subtopics.description: The remainder cycle in long division, and what it says about rational numbers.
subtopics.coverNote: Enrichment beyond the spec's wording: the remainder cycle in the division algorithm forces every fraction to terminate or recur, with cycle length below the denominator. Keep it light and unexamined; classification vocabulary lives on the structure topic's rational-and-irrational; prediction lives on which-fractions-terminate. Both tiers. (N10)

subtopics.title: Terminating decimals to fractions
subtopics.description: Converting a terminating decimal to a fraction by place value.
subtopics.coverNote: Converting terminating decimals to fractions by place value, e.g. 0.36 = 36/100 = 9/25, simplifying with the HCF; thousandths included; decimals above 1 to mixed numbers. N10 makes this both tiers; recurring decimals need the Higher algebraic method on the next page. (N10)

subtopics.title: Recurring decimals to fractions
subtopics.description: The algebraic subtraction method, including digits before the recurring block.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, N10's braced clause. The algebraic subtraction method: set x equal to the decimal, multiply by the power of ten matching the block length, subtract and solve; one- and two-digit blocks, plus digits before the block; converting back by division. Foundation stops at terminating decimals. (N10)

subtopics.title: Percentages and fractions
subtopics.description: Per cent as parts per hundred, converting a percentage to a fraction and back.
subtopics.coverNote: Per cent as parts per hundred; converting percentages to fractions in simplest form and back via hundredths or multiplying by 100, including 12.5 per cent and thirds. Decimal conversions live on the sibling page; percentage-of-amount methods live in the percentages group. Both tiers. (N12, R9)

subtopics.title: Percentages and decimals
subtopics.description: Converting between a percentage and a decimal by shifting two place columns.
subtopics.coverNote: Converting between percentages and decimals by shifting digits two place columns, including 175 per cent, 0.5 per cent and 12.5 per cent; multiplier language introduced here. Fraction conversions live on the sibling page; applying multipliers to amounts lives on percentage-multiplier. Both tiers. (N12, R9)

subtopics.title: Ordering fractions, decimals and percentages
subtopics.description: Ordering fractions, decimals and percentages by converting to one form.
subtopics.coverNote: Ordering mixed lists of fractions, decimals and percentages by converting everything to one form, usually decimals or percentages, and stating the original values in order. Assumes both conversion pages; symbols live on comparison-symbols; negative values live on ordering-negatives. Both tiers. (N1)

subtopics.title: Ordering negative values
subtopics.description: Ordering negatives, where the larger digit gives the smaller value.
subtopics.coverNote: Ordering negative fractions, decimals and percentages together, like -2/3, -0.7 and -70 per cent, where larger digits mean smaller values; number-line placement as justification. Assumes ordering-fdp conversions and the structure topic's directed-number work; positive lists live on ordering-fdp. Both tiers. (N1)

subtopics.title: Choosing the form to calculate in
subtopics.description: Whether a fraction, decimal or percentage makes a calculation shortest.
subtopics.coverNote: Choosing whichever of fraction, decimal or percentage makes a calculation shortest: 3/4 of 48 as a fraction, 17.5 per cent via decimals; justifying the choice in a sentence. No new conversions taught; all three conversion pages assumed; non-calculator efficiency is the point. Both tiers. (N2, N12)

subtopics.title: Percentages without a calculator
subtopics.description: Building a percentage of an amount from 50%, 25%, 10%, 5% and 1%.
subtopics.coverNote: Building any percentage of an amount from 50, 25, 10, 5 and 1 per cent, e.g. 17.5 per cent as 10 plus 5 plus 2.5; non-calculator money contexts. The one-step multiplier lives on percentage-multiplier; increases and decreases follow later in the group. Both tiers. (N12, R9)

subtopics.title: Percentage of an amount by multiplier
subtopics.description: A percentage of an amount in one step with a decimal multiplier.
subtopics.coverNote: Finding a percentage of an amount in one step with a decimal multiplier, including 17.5 per cent as 0.175 and percentages below 1 per cent; calculator allowed. The build-up method is the sibling page; multipliers above 1 live on percentages-over-100; change lives on percentage-increase-decrease. Both tiers. (N12, R9)

subtopics.title: Writing one quantity as a percentage of another
subtopics.description: One quantity as a percentage of another, and comparing different totals.
subtopics.coverNote: Writing one quantity as a percentage of another in common units, part over whole times 100; comparing scores out of different totals; answers over 100 allowed. Percentage change between a before and after value is a different method, on percentage-change. Both tiers. (N12, R9)

subtopics.title: Percentages above 100%
subtopics.description: Percentages greater than the whole, and the multipliers above 1 they give.
subtopics.coverNote: Percentages above 100 as amounts exceeding the whole, which R9 names explicitly at Foundation; multipliers above 1, like 140 per cent as 1.4; contexts such as 250 per cent of a cost. Assumes percentage-multiplier; repeated growth and compound interest live in the Ratio strand. Both tiers. (N12, R9)

subtopics.title: Percentage increase and decrease
subtopics.description: Increasing or decreasing a quantity by a percentage with one multiplier.
subtopics.coverNote: Increasing or decreasing an amount by a given percentage with one multiplier, times 1.15 or times 0.85, two-step method as backup; VAT, sales and wages. Finding the percentage change from two amounts lives on percentage-change; repeated and compound change lives in the Ratio strand. Both tiers. (N12, R9)

subtopics.title: Percentage change from two amounts
subtopics.description: Finding the percentage rise or fall from the change over the original.
subtopics.coverNote: Percentage change as change over original times 100: profit, loss and error from before-and-after amounts; choosing the original as denominator is the taught point. Applying a stated change lives on percentage-increase-decrease; undoing one lives on reverse-percentage; percentage error on measurements lives on Measures. Both tiers. (N12, R9)

subtopics.title: Reverse percentages
subtopics.description: Recovering the original amount by dividing by the multiplier.
subtopics.coverNote: Recovering the original amount after a known percentage change by dividing by the multiplier, which R9 names as finding the original value; prices before VAT or a sale. Confront the subtract-the-same-percentage error. Assumes percentage-increase-decrease; the fraction analogue lives on finding-the-whole. Both tiers. (N12, R9)

topics.verify:
**Defects**

1. **Ordering (Fractions as numbers)** — `fractions-on-a-number-line` places a *mixed number* on the line, but `mixed-numbers` introduces the form two pages later.
2. **Ordering (Fractions as numbers)** — `comparison-symbols` sits after `ordering-fractions`, so the symbols used to state a comparison arrive after the page that does the comparing.
3. **Ordering (cross-group)** — `reciprocals` includes the reciprocal of a decimal, but decimal-to-fraction conversion is not taught until `decimals-to-fractions`, four groups later.
4. **Bundling** — `ordering-fractions` carries three distinct comparison methods (common denominator, common numerator, benchmarking) on one page, out of step with the splitting used everywhere else in the list.
5. **Drill placement** — the fraction-arithmetic drill is anchored to `multiplying-dividing-mixed-numbers`, ahead of `adding-subtracting-negative-fractions` and `multiplying-dividing-negative-fractions`, which are also fraction arithmetic and fall inside its scope (`pages/practice-gcse-number-fraction-arithmetic.html` is documented in `/Users/joeltaylor/Documents/Code/demystifyingmaths/docs/syllabus-coverage.md:519` as "four operations with fractions and mixed numbers").
6. **Title/description mismatch** — `adding-subtracting-negative-fractions` is titled "Adding and subtracting negative fractions" but the description covers only sign placement and subtracting a negative; adding is never described.
7. **Minor inconsistency** — `fractions-to-decimals` teaches the conversion by *short division*, while `why-decimals-recur` explains the remainder cycle in *long division*; same procedure, two names, across consecutive pages.

No duplicate pages found. Check 5 (voice) is clean: all 38 descriptions are 13–17 words, British spelling throughout ("cancelling", "per cent", "practise/practice" used correctly), no marketing language.

subtopics.title: Comparing quantities in different units
subtopics.description: Ordering and adding quantities by converting to a common unit first.
subtopics.coverNote: Ordering, adding and subtracting quantities stated in different metric units by converting to a common unit first, e.g. 1.2 m plus 45 cm; choosing the cleanest common unit. Assumes metric-units; time needs base-60 care and lives in the time group. Both tiers. (N13)

subtopics.title: Money: pounds and pence

subtopics.title: Metric and imperial conversion
subtopics.description: Approximate equivalences for miles, pounds, pints and inches.
subtopics.coverNote: Approximate equivalences: 5 miles is about 8 km, 1 kg about 2.2 pounds, 1 pint about 568 ml, 1 inch about 2.5 cm; converting each way and choosing the factor's direction. Metric-metric conversion assumed; obscure imperial chains like furlongs stay out. Both tiers. (N13)

subtopics.title: Units of time
subtopics.description: Seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks and years, and month lengths.
subtopics.coverNote: Converting seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months and years, with month lengths and leap years; why 1.5 hours is 90 minutes, not 150. Clock notation lives on clock-times; durations on time-durations; the decimal-hours trap gets its own page for rate work. Both tiers. (N13)

subtopics.title: The 12-hour and 24-hour clock
subtopics.description: Writing the same time in both notations, and where midnight causes trouble.
subtopics.coverNote: Writing the same time in 12-hour am/pm and 24-hour notation and converting between them; midnight, midday, 00:00 and 12:00 as the trouble spots. Notation only: durations live on time-durations, timetables on timetables, and no arithmetic happens on this page. Both tiers. (N13)

subtopics.title: Finding a duration between two times
subtopics.description: Working out the time between two clock times by bridging to the next whole hour.
subtopics.coverNote: Finding the duration between two clock times by bridging to the next whole hour, including spans across midday and midnight; finding a start or end time from a duration. Assumes clock-times; the 2.30-on-a-calculator trap lives on decimal-hours; timetable reading lives on timetables. Both tiers. (N13)

subtopics.title: Reading timetables
subtopics.description: Journey and waiting times from a timetable, and choosing a service.
subtopics.coverNote: Reading bus and train timetables in 24-hour notation: journey times down a column, waiting times, catching the latest service that arrives by a deadline. Assumes time-durations; drawing or interpreting distance-time graphs belongs to the Ratio strand's graph work, not here. Both tiers. (N13)

subtopics.title: Decimal hours
subtopics.description: Converting between hours and minutes and decimal hours for rate work.
subtopics.coverNote: Converting between hours-and-minutes and decimal hours in both directions: 2 h 45 min is 2.75 h, 0.4 h is 24 minutes; why keying 2.30 for 2 h 30 min fails. Needed before speed work; the speed-distance-time relationship itself lives in the Ratio strand. Both tiers. (N13)

subtopics.title: Converting compound units
subtopics.description: Changing m/s into km/h by converting numerator and denominator separately.
subtopics.coverNote: Converting compound units by handling numerator and denominator separately: m/s to km/h, pounds per kg to pence per g; tracking which way each factor acts. Unit conversion only: defining and calculating speed, density and pressure lives in the Ratio strand under R11, so cross-reference. Both tiers. (N13, R1)

subtopics.title: Compound units with a squared or cubed part
subtopics.description: Converting grams per cubic centimetre to kilograms per cubic metre.
subtopics.coverNote: Both tiers, N13 is unbraced: converting compound units whose denominator carries a power, g per cm cubed to kg per m cubed, applying the cubed factor to the bottom. Assumes compound-units and area-volume-units; density calculation itself lives in the Ratio strand. (N13, R1)

subtopics.title: Reading scales
subtopics.description: What one division is worth on a ruler, jug, dial or weighing scale.
subtopics.coverNote: Working out what one division is worth on rulers, jugs, dials and weighing scales, then reading values that sit between labelled marks; estimating between divisions. Choosing which unit fits lives on sensible-units; the half-a-division accuracy idea is developed on measurement-accuracy. Both tiers. (N13)

subtopics.title: Choosing a sensible unit
subtopics.description: Picking the unit that fits the quantity, so a door is measured in metres.
subtopics.coverNote: Choosing the unit that fits a quantity: metres for a door, millilitres for a spoon, tonnes for a lorry; metric preferred, imperial where everyday. Estimating the actual size of something lives on estimating-measures; conversion arithmetic lives on metric-units. Both tiers. (N13)

subtopics.title: Estimating everyday measurements
subtopics.description: Estimating a length, mass or capacity against a quantity you already know.
subtopics.coverNote: Estimating lengths, masses and capacities by benchmarking against known quantities: a door about 2 m, a bag of sugar 1 kg, a mug about 300 ml; sanity-checking stated claims. Choosing the unit lives on sensible-units; estimating calculations rather than quantities lives on estimating-calculations. Both tiers. (N13, N14)

subtopics.title: Rounding to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand
subtopics.description: Rounding to a stated power of ten, keeping the zeros that hold the place values.
subtopics.coverNote: Rounding integers and decimals to the nearest ten, hundred, thousand and whole number, keeping place-holding zeros, e.g. 4972 to 4970; the halfway-rounds-up convention. Decimal places and significant figures get sibling pages; the interval a rounded value came from lives in the error-intervals group. Both tiers. (N15)

subtopics.title: Rounding to decimal places
subtopics.description: Rounding a decimal to a stated number of places from the next digit only.
subtopics.coverNote: Rounding decimals to one, two or three decimal places by inspecting only the next digit, including nines carrying over like 2.397 to 2.40, and keeping that trailing zero. Significant figures live on the sibling page; the two-decimal money convention lives on money-units. Both tiers. (N15)

subtopics.title: Rounding negative numbers
subtopics.description: Rounding along the number line, so −3.47 rounds to −3.5 and −3.44 to −3.4.
subtopics.coverNote: Rounding negatives along the number line, so -3.47 to one decimal place is -3.5 and -3.44 is -3.4; showing where ignore-the-sign shortcuts agree and why the number-line justification is safer. Assumes rounding-decimal-places; error intervals for negatives stay out of scope. Both tiers. (N15)

subtopics.title: Rounding to significant figures
subtopics.description: Finding the first significant figure and rounding from there.
subtopics.coverNote: Finding the first significant figure of large and small numbers and rounding to one, two or three significant figures, e.g. 0.004508 to 0.0045; one-significant-figure rounding feeds estimation. Zero subtleties live on significant-figure-zeros; estimating whole calculations lives on estimating-calculations. Both tiers. (N15)

subtopics.title: Zeros and significant figures
subtopics.description: Leading zeros never count, and zeros lost by rounding are written back.
subtopics.coverNote: The zero rules: leading zeros never significant, sandwiched zeros significant, and zeros lost in rounding written back as place holders, so 20468 to one significant figure is 20000. Assumes significant-figures; stating how many significant figures a given value has is included. Both tiers. (N15)

subtopics.title: Truncation
subtopics.description: Cutting a number off at a decimal place or significant figure, not rounding.
subtopics.coverNote: Truncating at a stated decimal place or significant figure by cutting digits without rounding, e.g. 3.79 truncates to 3.7; contexts that truncate naturally, such as stating ages. Contrast with rounding throughout; the interval a truncated value came from lives on error-intervals-truncation. Both tiers. (N15)

subtopics.title: When the context forces the direction
subtopics.description: Rounding up regardless of the digits when the context demands it.
subtopics.coverNote: Contexts that force the rounding direction whatever the digits say: coaches, boxes and tins round up, complete items round down; identifying the direction from the wording. The arithmetic-remainder version lives on the structure topic's interpreting-remainders; how many figures to keep lives on choosing-accuracy. Both tiers. (N15)

subtopics.title: Choosing the accuracy of a final answer
subtopics.description: How many figures an answer should carry, given the accuracy of the inputs.
subtopics.coverNote: Deciding how many figures a final answer should carry from the accuracy of the inputs and the context, and why copying eight calculator digits misleads. Direction-forced rounding lives on rounding-in-context; the Higher, bounds-justified version of this decision lives on suitable-accuracy-bounds. Both tiers. (N15)

subtopics.title: Rounding during a calculation
subtopics.description: Why intermediate values are kept at full accuracy until the final answer.
subtopics.coverNote: Why intermediate values are held at full accuracy and rounding waits for the final answer, with examples where mid-way rounding visibly shifts the result; the ANS-key workflow. Key mechanics live on the structure topic's calculator-ans-memory, so cross-reference; multi-step calculator questions are the format. Both tiers. (N14, N15)

subtopics.title: Estimating by rounding to one significant figure
subtopics.description: Rounding every number to one significant figure, then calculating exactly.
subtopics.coverNote: Estimating by rounding every value to one significant figure and working the simplified calculation exactly, including fraction-bar layouts like 48.6 times 2.9 over 0.51, and division by a decimal below one enlarging. Whether the estimate is high or low lives on over-under-estimates. Both tiers. (N14)

subtopics.title: Over-estimates and under-estimates
subtopics.description: Judging each rounding by the role its number plays in the calculation.
subtopics.coverNote: Deciding whether an estimate is an over- or under-estimate from the role each rounded number plays: a divisor rounded down inflates the result; arguing each value separately. Assumes estimating-calculations; rigorous greatest-and-least arithmetic is Higher, in the calculating-with-bounds group. Both tiers. (N14)

subtopics.title: Estimating powers and roots
subtopics.description: Trapping a number between the nearest squares or cubes to estimate its root.
subtopics.coverNote: Trapping root 40 between root 36 and root 49 to place it between 6 and 7, refining to one decimal place, and estimating powers by rounding the base. Higher only, N6 braces estimating powers and roots; exact roots live on the structure topic. (N6, N14)

subtopics.title: Checking an answer is sensible
subtopics.description: Testing a result against an estimate, the context, and the inverse operation.
subtopics.coverNote: Checking a result against a one-significant-figure estimate, against context (a 400 mph cyclist fails), and by the inverse operation; N14 includes checking answers obtained using technology. Inverse mechanics live on the structure topic's checking-with-inverses; estimation mechanics on estimating-calculations. Both tiers. (N3, N14)

subtopics.title: Error intervals from rounding
subtopics.description: The interval a rounded value came from, half a unit either side.
subtopics.coverNote: Writing the error interval of a value rounded to a place value or decimal places, half a unit either side with strict inequality on top, e.g. 5.65 at-most x < 5.75; N15 names inequality notation for these intervals. Truncation and significant-figure versions get sibling pages. Both tiers. (N15)

subtopics.title: Why a measurement is never exact
subtopics.description: Why a reading is only ever accurate to half the smallest division on the scale.
subtopics.coverNote: Why a physical reading is accurate only to half the smallest scale division, so every measurement stands for an interval: 36 cm to the nearest cm means 35.5 to 36.5. Motivates the group; interval-writing mechanics live on error-intervals-rounding; instrument reading lives on reading-scales. Both tiers. (N15)

subtopics.title: Error intervals from significant figures
subtopics.description: Finding the rounding unit from the last significant figure, then the interval.
subtopics.coverNote: Error intervals of values rounded to significant figures: find the place value of the last significant figure, then take half a unit either side, e.g. 4300 to two significant figures gives 4250 at-most x < 4350; small decimals included. Assumes significant-figures and error-intervals-rounding. Both tiers. (N15)

subtopics.title: Error intervals from truncation
subtopics.description: Why a truncated value is its own lower bound, with an interval one unit wide.
subtopics.coverNote: Error intervals of truncated values, which N15 names alongside rounding: the value is its own lower bound and the interval spans one whole unit, so 7.3 truncated means 7.3 at-most x < 7.4; contrast with the rounding interval directly. Assumes truncation; counted quantities live on discrete-bounds. Both tiers. (N15)

subtopics.title: Working back from an interval
subtopics.description: Recovering the stated value and its accuracy from an error interval.
subtopics.coverNote: Working back from a stated interval to the rounded value and the accuracy used, e.g. 245 at-most x < 255 means 250 to the nearest ten; spotting truncation from the value sitting at the lower end. Assumes all three interval pages; no arithmetic on bounds here. Both tiers. (N15)

subtopics.title: Bounds of discrete quantities
subtopics.description: Greatest and least possible values when a quantity counts whole items.
subtopics.coverNote: Both tiers, N15's error-interval clause is unbraced: greatest and least possible values of counted quantities, where bounds are whole units and the maximum is attainable, so 300 people to the nearest hundred means 250 to 349 inclusive. Continuous rounded values live on error-intervals-rounding. (N15)

subtopics.title: Maximum error and percentage error
subtopics.description: The greatest possible error as a percentage of the measurement.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher page. The greatest possible error as half the rounding unit, then expressed as a percentage of the stated measurement; comparing the reliability of two measurements. Not named in N1-N16, so treat as enrichment bridging into bounds; assumes error-intervals-rounding and the FDP topic's percentage-change. (N15, N16)

subtopics.title: Bounds in addition and subtraction
subtopics.description: Why the greatest difference pairs an upper bound with a lower bound.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, N16's braced bounds clause. Upper and lower bounds of sums and differences: the greatest difference pairs one value's upper bound with the other's lower; perimeter and combined-mass contexts. Assumes error-intervals-rounding; products and quotients live on bounds-multiply-divide. (N16)

subtopics.title: Bounds in multiplication and division
subtopics.description: Why the largest quotient divides upper by lower, and the smallest reverses it.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Bounds of products and quotients: the greatest quotient divides upper by lower, the least reverses it; tabulating both bounds of every value before choosing. Assumes bounds-add-subtract; speed, density and pressure applications live on bounds-compound-measures; geometry on bounds-geometry. (N16)

subtopics.title: Bounds in compound measures
subtopics.description: The bound each quantity takes in a speed, density or pressure calculation.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Choosing which bound each quantity takes inside speed, density and pressure calculations, e.g. greatest speed is greatest distance over least time; unit handling assumed from compound-units. The formulas themselves live in the Ratio strand; decision arguments live on bounds-decision-problems. (N16)

subtopics.title: Bounds in area, volume and Pythagoras
subtopics.description: Pushing upper and lower bounds through a geometric formula to bound the result.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Pushing bounds through geometric formulas: area, volume, Pythagoras and trigonometry, bounding each input first, e.g. the greatest hypotenuse takes both upper bounds; keep pi exact. Assumes bounds-multiply-divide; whether something definitely fits lives on bounds-decision-problems. (N16)

subtopics.title: Deciding from the worst case
subtopics.description: Whether something definitely fits, tested on the least favourable bounds.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Yes-or-no decisions argued from the worst case: does the ladder definitely reach, does the lift definitely carry them, testing the least favourable pair of bounds and writing the comparison sentence examiners want. Assumes every earlier bounds page; no new bound arithmetic. (N16)

subtopics.title: A suitable degree of accuracy from bounds
subtopics.description: Quoting an answer only to the accuracy where its bounds still agree.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Quoting an answer to a suitable degree of accuracy by computing upper and lower bounds and keeping only the figures on which both agree, e.g. bounds 8.63 and 8.68 justify 8.6. Assumes bounds arithmetic; the Foundation judgement version lives on choosing-accuracy. (N15, N16)

topics.verify:
1. **`error-intervals-rounding` / `measurement-accuracy` teach the same rule.** Both are the "half a unit / half the smallest division" idea; the second adds only that the value came from an instrument rather than a rounding instruction.

2. **`measurement-accuracy` is placed after the page that depends on it** (Error intervals group, position 2). "Why a measurement is never exact" is the motivation for error intervals, so it sits after the technique it justifies.

3. **`percentage-error` bundles a restatement with a new method.** "The greatest possible error in a rounded measurement" is half a unit — already established by `error-intervals-rounding` — carried on the same page as the separate percentage-of-measurement calculation.

4. **`money-units` bundles two different things.** Pounds↔pence conversion and the two-decimal-place writing convention are unrelated methods sharing one page.

Minor: `sensible-units` and `estimating-measures` both hang on the same door benchmark, which makes two adjacent pages read as one.

drills.title: Place value in integers and decimals
drills.description: What each digit is worth in integers and decimals, and zeros as place-holders.
drills.skill: What each digit is worth in integers and decimals, and zeros as place-holders.
drills.scope: Digit values in integers to millions and decimals to thousandths; zeros as place-holders; writing numbers in words and figures; stating the value of a named digit. Ordering and comparing live on the sibling ordering-numbers page; rounding lives on Measures and accuracy. Both tiers. (N2)
sections: Digit values — state the value of a named digit in integers to millions and decimals to thousandths (4 questions).
Place-holders — identify or complete numbers where zeros hold whole-number or decimal places (4 questions).
Words and figures — convert between words and figures, including internal zeros and decimal parts (4 questions).

drills.title: Ordering integers, decimals and negatives
drills.description: Ordering numbers, including negatives and decimals of different lengths.
drills.skill: Ordering numbers, including negatives and decimals of different lengths.
drills.scope: Ordering integers, decimals of different lengths and negatives, ascending and descending, with number-line placement; padding decimals to equal length; temperature contexts. The symbols themselves live on inequality-symbols; ordering fractions and percentages lives in the FDP topic; standard-form ordering has its own page. Both tiers. (N1)
sections: Decimal order — choose the smallest or largest from decimals of different lengths (4 questions).
Negative order — choose correctly ordered lists containing positive and negative integers and decimals (4 questions).
Number lines and contexts — order values ascending or descending in number-line and temperature contexts (4 questions).

drills.title: The inequality symbols
drills.description: The less-than, greater-than, at-most, at-least and not-equal signs.
drills.skill: The less-than, greater-than, at-most, at-least and not-equal signs.
drills.scope: Reading and writing the six DfE symbols =, not-equal, <, >, at-most and at-least between numbers, including negatives and decimals; which two allow equality; listing integers satisfying a statement like -2 < n at-most 3. Solving inequalities is Algebra; error-interval notation lives on Measures. Both tiers. (N1)
sections: Basic comparisons — choose =, < or > between integers, decimals and negative numbers (4 questions).
Extended symbols — translate at most, at least and not equal into ≤, ≥ and ≠, including which allow equality (4 questions).
Integer solutions — select the integers satisfying statements such as −2 < n ≤ 3 (4 questions).

drills.title: Column addition
drills.description: Adding integers and decimals in columns, lining up the point and carrying.
drills.skill: Adding integers and decimals in columns, lining up the point and carrying.
drills.scope: Column addition of integers and decimals of different lengths, carrying between columns, aligning the point, padding with zeros; money and measure contexts. Subtraction lives on column-subtraction; estimation checks live on Measures; negative operands live on adding-subtracting-negatives. Both tiers. (N2)
sections: Fluency — add integers and decimals of different lengths by aligning place values and padding zeros (4 questions).
Carrying — add values that require carrying through one or more columns (4 questions).
Application — solve addition-only money and measure problems, with units fixed by the prompt (4 questions).

drills.title: Column subtraction
drills.description: Subtracting in columns with exchange, lining up decimals of different lengths.
drills.skill: Subtracting in columns with exchange, lining up decimals of different lengths.
drills.scope: Column subtraction of integers and decimals with exchange, aligning points and padding shorter decimals, e.g. 12 - 3.475; change and difference contexts. Exchanges that must pass through zero digits get the sibling page; answers below zero live on adding-subtracting-negatives. Both tiers. (N2)
sections: Fluency — subtract integers and decimals of different lengths by aligning place values and padding zeros (4 questions).
Exchange — subtract with ordinary single-column exchanges, excluding any exchange that must pass through a zero (4 questions).
Application — solve change and difference problems with non-negative answers and no across-zero exchange (4 questions).

drills.title: Exchanging across zeros
drills.description: Subtracting when a column holds a zero, and where the exchange comes from.
drills.skill: Subtracting when a column holds a zero, and where the exchange comes from.
drills.scope: Subtractions like 4.03 - 1.276 and 3000 - 847 where the exchange must travel through one or more zeros, showing where each borrowed unit comes from and the reindexed digits. Assumes column-subtraction; do not reteach basic single-column exchange here. Both tiers. (N2)
sections: Integers — subtract values such as 3000 − 847 where an exchange passes through one or more zeros (4 questions).
Decimals — subtract values such as 4.03 − 1.276 with zero place-holders and chained exchange (4 questions).
Application — solve subtraction contexts whose written method requires an exchange across zeros (4 questions).

drills.title: Long multiplication
drills.description: Multiplying multi-digit integers, and the place-holder zero in the second row.
drills.skill: Multiplying multi-digit integers, and the place-holder zero in the second row.
drills.scope: Long multiplication of two- and three-digit integers with the place-holder zero in each later row; grid method as backup; worded cost and area contexts. Decimal operands live on multiplying-decimals; estimation as a check lives on Measures estimating-calculations. Both tiers. (N2)
sections: Fluency — multiply two- and three-digit integers by two-digit integers using long multiplication (4 questions).
Structure — complete missing partial products and place-holder zeros in later rows (4 questions).
Application — solve integer-only cost and area problems by long multiplication (4 questions).

drills.title: Short division
drills.description: Dividing by a one-digit number, carrying each remainder into the next digit.
drills.skill: Dividing by a one-digit number, carrying each remainder into the next digit.
drills.scope: Short division of integers and decimals by one-digit divisors, carrying remainders into the next digit and continuing past the point for exact decimal answers. Deciding what a leftover means lives on interpreting-remainders; two-digit divisors live on long-division. Both tiers. (N2)
sections: Fluency — divide integer and decimal dividends by one-digit divisors, carrying into the next place (4 questions).
Exact decimals — continue past the decimal point until a one-digit division terminates exactly (4 questions).
Structure — complete missing quotient digits or carried remainders in short-division layouts (4 questions).

drills.title: Interpreting a remainder
drills.description: Whether a worded answer wants a remainder, a decimal, a fraction or rounding.
drills.skill: Whether a worded answer wants a remainder, a decimal, a fraction or rounding.
drills.scope: Worded division answers: choosing between remainder form, exact decimal, fraction, and rounding up or down in context (coaches, boxes, tickets). One-digit divisors here; the context-forced rounding direction recurs on Measures rounding-in-context, so cross-reference rather than duplicate. Both tiers. (N2)
sections: Answer forms — express one-digit divisions as a remainder, exact decimal or fraction as requested (4 questions).
Directed rounding — decide whether a one-digit division context requires rounding up or down (4 questions).
Mixed contexts — choose the appropriate answer for coaches, boxes, tickets and leftovers; the decision is the catch (4 questions).

drills.title: Long division
drills.description: Dividing by a two-digit number, continuing past the point for an exact answer.
drills.skill: Dividing by a two-digit number, continuing past the point for an exact answer.
drills.scope: Long division by two-digit divisors, integer and decimal dividends, continuing past the point for exact decimal answers; layout, subtracting multiples, and a listed multiples crib. Decimal divisors live on dividing-by-decimals; remainder interpretation lives on interpreting-remainders. Both tiers. (N2)
sections: Integer quotients — divide by two-digit integer divisors using listed multiples and long division (4 questions).
Exact decimals — divide integer or decimal dividends and continue past the point to an exact answer (4 questions).
Structure and application — complete missing long-division steps or solve a context with a two-digit divisor (4 questions).

drills.title: Using a given calculation
drills.description: Deducing new decimal products and quotients from one stated calculation, without recalculating.
drills.skill: Deducing new products and quotients from a stated calculation by tracking powers of ten.
sections: Fluency — scaling a stated integer product by powers of ten, such as 4.3 × 26 from a given 43 × 26 (4 questions).
Quotients — deducing divisions from the stated fact, in both directions (4 questions).
Reversed deductions — finding a missing factor or dividend from the stated fact, where blind digit-shifting gives the wrong power of ten (4 questions).
drills.scope: From a stated fact like 43 x 26 = 1118, deducing related products, quotients and missing factors such as 4.3 x 2.6 and 1118 / 4.3 by tracking powers of ten; no recalculating. Estimating unrelated calculations lives on Measures estimating-calculations. Both tiers. (N2, N3)

drills.title: Index notation and powers
drills.description: What the base and index mean, and writing repeated multiplication as a power.
drills.skill: What the base and index mean, and writing repeated multiplication as a power.
drills.scope: Meaning of base and index for positive integer powers; writing repeated multiplication as a power and back; evaluating squares, cubes and small powers like 2 to the 5 without a calculator. The index laws live in their own group; algebraic indices live in Algebra. Both tiers. (N6)
sections: Fluency — direct questions on index notation and powers, limited to this lesson's stated scope (4 questions).
Application — use the same skill in unfamiliar or contextual questions without introducing a later method (4 questions).
Check — questions built around the exclusions and likely misconceptions named in the lesson brief (4 questions).

drills.title: Recognising powers of a number
